title: Server Software Component: Web Shell
summary: A web shell is a server-side script planted in a web-accessible location so that ordinary HTTP requests become a remote control channel. The adversary typically arrives through a vulnerable web application, a file upload feature, or stolen administrative access, then writes a small script in the language the server already executes, such as PHP, ASP, ASP.NET, or Java. Because the file sits in the web root, the web server runs it with the privileges of the web account and the operator reaches it over the same ports as normal browsing traffic. Capabilities range from a single command parameter to a full browsing console that reads and writes files, runs system commands, and pivots to internal hosts. Some tools pair the server script with a dedicated client, for example the China Chopper client. Detection combines three views: file system integrity, where new or modified script files appear in web directories outside a deployment window; web access logs, where requests to that script repeat with unusual parameters, user agents, or sizes; and process ancestry, where the web server process spawns command interpreters or network utilities. Web shells often survive patching of the original entry point, so eradicating the vulnerability without removing the script leaves the attacker access.

beginner.definition: A web shell is a small script that an attacker hides on the server of a website. When the attacker opens a special web address, the script runs and lets them give orders to the machine. It is called a shell because it works like a command line that the attacker reaches through a normal web browser.
beginner.whyItMatters: Web servers are usually reachable from the internet, so the attacker can return at any time from anywhere. Their traffic travels on the same ports as ordinary visitors, which makes it hard to block without breaking the website. A web shell often keeps working even after the original flaw is patched, so the attacker stays inside. From the web server they can often reach databases and internal systems.
howItWorks: The attacker finds a way to place a file on the web server, such as a file upload feature or a known flaw.
They write a short script in a language the web server already runs, like PHP or ASP.
They open the script through a normal web address and send instructions in the request.
The web server runs the script with its own permissions and returns the result as a web page.
The script grows into a console for reading files, running commands and reaching other systems.
The attacker may use a matching client program that makes sending these requests fast and easy.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel front desk that accepts written requests from guests and passes them to staff. Someone slips an extra instruction card into the desk drawer that says: if a guest asks about the weather, also hand over the master key. Any guest can then use one harmless question to get the key, and the desk still works normally for everyone else.
takeaways: A web shell is a file, so file integrity checks on web folders matter.
Repeated odd requests to one script in your web logs are a strong clue.
Patching the entry flaw is not enough while the planted script is still there.

objectives: Explain what a web shell is and how a web request becomes command execution.
Describe how a web shell is planted using uploads, flaws, or stolen access.
Identify the file, log and process evidence a web shell leaves behind.
Distinguish a legitimate web script from an attacker-planted one.
Outline containment steps that remove the script and the entry path together.
